warmup.q: A payments table is stored as one directory per day, payments/dt=2026-11-01/ to payments/dt=2026-11-30/. A query filters WHERE created_at >= '2026-11-29'. How many day directories does the engine read?
options: 2, because created_at and dt hold the same dates
All 30, because the filter isn't on the partition column
None, because created_at isn't stored in the files
warmup.why: The engine skips directories by matching the filter against the dt values in their names. It has no way to know that created_at and dt agree, so it opens every file and filters rows inside them. Same answer, thirty times the reading. Adding dt >= '2026-11-29' to the query fixes it.

sections.h: A Hive table is a directory plus a schema stored somewhere else
sections.html:
Facebook's Hive paper (2009) starts from a familiar spot. The data sat as files in Hadoop, on HDFS, the replicated file system from lesson 2. Every question about it needed a custom MapReduce program, which the paper calls low level and hard to maintain and reuse. The analysts knew SQL. So ask what it would take to run this against a folder of files:

SELECT status, count(*) FROM payments GROUP BY status;

SQL needs facts that a folder doesn't have. It needs a name for the data, payments. It needs the columns and their types, called the schema, so that status means something. And it needs to know where the files are and how to read them: CSV, Parquet (the column-by-column format from lesson 1), or something else.

Version 1: put all of that into every query. DuckDB, the single-machine engine from lesson 1, lets you do exactly that:

SELECT status, count(*)
FROM read_parquet('/lake/payments/*.parquet')   -- where the files are, and their format
GROUP BY status;

That works for one person. It breaks when fifty analysts each copy the path, the format and the column types into their own queries. Move the folder and every query breaks, and nobody can tell which folders are tables.

Version 2: write the description down once, in a shared place, under a name. That is what Hive did. Facebook described it in 2009: analysts wrote SQL (in a dialect called HiveQL), and Hive compiled each query into MapReduce jobs. Facebook's warehouse already held several thousand Hive tables and over 700 TB. A Hive table is two things kept apart. The files sit in one directory per table. The description (schema, file format, the directory's location) sits in a separate database called the metastore. A query joins the two when it runs. Keep this picture for the whole lesson: a name in the metastore that points at a directory full of files. The figure below draws it.

Keeping the two apart has a consequence. Oracle checks every row against the table definition when you insert it: a string like '12.50 EUR' in a NUMBER column fails right there. Hive checks nothing on the way in. Any job that drops a file into the directory has added rows, without an INSERT. A file with the wrong types lands without complaint, and the error shows up later, when a query reads it. This is schema on read. It made loading data trivial, and it moved the cost of bad data to whoever reads it.

Hive also has two kinds of table. It owns the files of a managed table, so DROP TABLE deletes them. It only points at the files of an external table, so DROP TABLE deletes the description and leaves the files. Data lakes, shared folders of files that many tools read, mostly use external tables.

Hive the engine is legacy now. The project declared its 1.x, 2.x and 3.x lines end of life in 2024, and Hive 4.2.1 came out in August 2026, needing JDK 21. Its ideas are everywhere, though. Spark, Trino and DuckDB all read Hive-style tables, and the metastore is still a common catalog, the general name for a service that maps table names to their descriptions. This lesson's demos use DuckDB and Spark's built-in catalog, so you need no Hive install.

try.title: Add rows by copying files
steps: From the labs folder, run SchemaOnReadDemo. It treats a directory as a table through a DuckDB view (a saved query with a name) over *.parquet.
Watch the row count after the third file lands. Nobody ran INSERT.
Predict before you read the last line: the fourth file was written without an error. What happens to the next query?

code.title: SchemaOnReadDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.bigdata.l03.demo import java.io.File import java.sql.Connection import java.sql.DriverManager /** * A "table" that is only a directory of files plus a schema. Adding a file adds rows, and a bad * file is only noticed when a query reads it. */ fun main() { val dir = File("build/l03/raw/payments").apply { deleteRecursively(); mkdirs() } DriverManager.getConnection("jdbc:duckdb:").use { c -> // two batches land as files; nobody runs INSERT batch(c, File(dir, "batch-1.parquet"), from = 0) batch(c, File(dir, "batch-2.parquet"), from = 1_000) c.run("CREATE VIEW payments AS SELECT * FROM read_parquet('${dir.absolutePath}/*.parquet')") println("2 files: " + c.query("SELECT count(*), sum(amount_cents) FROM payments")) batch(c, File(dir, "batch-3.parquet"), from = 2_000) println("3 files: " + c.query("SELECT count(*), sum(amount_cents) FROM payments")) // an upstream job changes amount_cents to text like '12.50 EUR'; writing the file works fine c.run("COPY (SELECT 3000 AS payment_id, '12.50 EUR' AS amount_cents) TO '${File(dir, "batch-4.parquet").absolutePath}' (FORMAT parquet)") println("4 files: " + runCatching { c.query("SELECT count(*), sum(amount_cents) FROM payments") } .getOrElse { "query failed: " + it.message!!.lineSequence().first() }) } } private fun batch(c: Connection, file: File, from: Int) = c.run("COPY (SELECT i AS payment_id, (i % 997) * 100 AS amount_cents FROM range($from, ${from + 1_000}) t(i)) TO '${file.absolutePath}' (FORMAT parquet)") private fun Connection.run(sql: String) = createStatement().use { it.execute(sql) } private fun Connection.query(sql: String): String = createStatement().use { s -> s.executeQuery(sql).use { rs -> rs.next(); (1..rs.metaData.columnCount).joinToString(", ") { "${rs.metaData.getColumnLabel(it)} = ${rs.getString(it)}" } } }

try.expect:
2 files:  count_star() = 2000, sum(amount_cents) = 99302700
3 files:  count_star() = 3000, sum(amount_cents) = 148955400
4 files:  query failed: Conversion Error: Error while reading file "/.../bigdata/build/l03/raw/payments/batch-4.parquet": failed to cast column "amount_cents" from type VARCHAR to BIGINT: : Could not convert string '12.50 EUR' to INT64

(The path is trimmed.) The third file added 1,000 rows by existing. The fourth file was accepted when it was written, and the error appears only when a query reads it. Every query that touches amount_cents now fails, not just the bad rows, until someone finds and removes that file.

sections.html:
A payments table grows by one day of data every day, and most questions are about recent days: yesterday's settlements, last week's declines. With one directory for the whole table, every query reads every file. After three years, a question about yesterday reads 1,095 days of data to use one of them.

The fix is to split the table's directory into subdirectories, one per day, and name each one after its value:

payments/
  dt=2026-11-01/
    part-00000-....snappy.parquet
    part-00001-....snappy.parquet
  dt=2026-11-02/
    part-00000-....snappy.parquet
  ...

Each subdirectory is a partition of the table, and dt is the partition column. The name holds both the column and the value, dt=2026-11-02, so any reader can rebuild the column from the path alone. In fact the value lives only in the path. When Spark writes with partitionBy("dt"), it removes the dt column from the rows and puts the value into the directory name instead. When an engine reads the table, it turns dt=2026-11-02 back into a column. Spark calls this partition discovery, and DuckDB calls it hive_partitioning.

The payoff is partition pruning. A query with WHERE dt = '2026-11-03' skips every other directory without opening a single file. With three years of days in the table, that query reads one day out of about a thousand. It is lesson 2's data locality pushed one step further: rather than moving the code to the data, don't go near data you don't need.

Pruning works only on the partition column itself. A filter on created_at may cover exactly the same day, but the engine can't know that from the directory names, so it opens every file. (It can still skip parts of each file using statistics; that's lesson 4.) Iceberg, a table format covered in lesson 9, removes this trap with hidden partitioning.

So pick partition columns that queries filter on and that have few distinct values. Day is the classic choice: three years is about a thousand directories. Partition by merchant_id as well, with 500,000 merchants, and you get 500 million directories, most holding one tiny file.

try.title: Make DuckDB skip six days
steps: Run PartitionPruningDemo. Spark writes a week of payments with partitionBy("dt"), then DuckDB plans two queries for the same day.
Look at the file paths it prints: where is dt?
Predict before the last two lines: how many files does each query open?

code.title: PartitionPruningDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.bigdata.l03.demo import org.apache.spark.sql.SaveMode import java.io.File import java.sql.DriverManager /** * Spark writes a week of payments as a Hive-style table, one directory per day. * Then DuckDB plans two queries for the same day and says how many files each would open. */ fun main() { val lake = File("build/l03/lake") val spark = demoSpark() demoPayments(spark).write().mode(SaveMode.Overwrite).partitionBy("dt").parquet(lake.absolutePath) spark.stop() val files = dataFiles(lake) println("%d files in %d directories, for example:".format(files.size, lake.listFiles { f -> f.isDirectory }!!.size)) files.take(3).forEach { println(" $it") } val scan = "read_parquet('${lake.absolutePath}/**/*.parquet', hive_partitioning = true)" DriverManager.getConnection("jdbc:duckdb:").use { c -> for (where in listOf("dt = '2026-11-03'", "created_at::DATE = DATE '2026-11-03'")) { val sql = "SELECT sum(amount_cents) FROM $scan WHERE $where" val plan = c.createStatement().use { s -> s.executeQuery("EXPLAIN $sql").use { rs -> rs.next(); rs.getString(2) } } // DuckDB prints "Scanning Files: n/total" only when it can skip files by their path val scanning = Regex("""Scanning Files: (\d+/\d+)""").find(plan)?.groupValues?.get(1) ?: "all ${files.size}" println("WHERE %-38s -> opens %s files".format(where, scanning)) } } }

try.expect:
8 files in 7 directories, for example:
  dt=2026-11-01/part-00000-509cf1d0-d6f7-4a94-8825-5bd91afbb939.c000.snappy.parquet
  dt=2026-11-02/part-00000-509cf1d0-d6f7-4a94-8825-5bd91afbb939.c000.snappy.parquet
  dt=2026-11-03/part-00000-509cf1d0-d6f7-4a94-8825-5bd91afbb939.c000.snappy.parquet
WHERE dt = '2026-11-03'                      -> opens 1/8 files
WHERE created_at::DATE = DATE '2026-11-03'   -> opens all 8 files

The file name changes every run. One day has two files because its rows came from both of Spark's two tasks. The dt filter opens one file. The created_at filter returns the same total and opens all eight. DuckDB prints a Scanning Files line only when it can skip files by their path, so a missing line means it reads them all.

sections.h: The metastore turns a table name into a list of directories
sections.html:
Pruning needs a list of the partitions that exist. The engine could build it by listing the table's directory before every query. On a laptop that takes microseconds. On S3, the object store from lesson 2, a listing returns at most 1,000 names per request. A table with 30,000 day and hour directories costs 30 requests, one after another, before any data is read. Hive's answer was to keep the partition list in the metastore, next to the schema.

The Hive Metastore (HMS) is a service with a relational database behind it. Clients talk to it over Thrift, a remote procedure call protocol similar to gRPC, on port 9083 by default. The database is Derby for quick tests, and MySQL, MariaDB, Postgres, Oracle or SQL Server in real use. For every table it stores the columns and types, the file format, the location, and one entry per partition with that partition's directory. Since Hive 3.0 it can also run on its own, without the rest of Hive, for engines such as Spark and Trino that only need the catalog.

Planning a query on a partitioned table then goes like this. The engine asks the metastore for the table and gets the schema and location. It passes the filter on the partition column along, and the metastore returns only the matching partitions, straight from its own database tables. Then the engine lists the files in those directories and reads them. The stepper below walks through it.

Notice where the truth now lives: in the metastore's partition list, not in the directories. A job that writes dt=2026-11-08/ straight to storage has written data that no query will find, because the metastore has no entry for it. The data looks lost until someone runs one of these:

ALTER TABLE payments ADD PARTITION (dt = '2026-11-08');   -- register one directory
MSCK REPAIR TABLE payments;                                -- list the location, add every missing one

MSCK REPAIR TABLE lists the whole table location, which is slow for a big table on S3, so pipelines usually add each partition right after they write it. Spark supports both statements. Its built-in catalog acts like a metastore even without Hive: a table created over existing directories starts with zero partitions.

try.title: Lose a day and find it again
steps: Run MetastoreDemo. It registers the lake from the previous Try it as a table in Spark's catalog, which plays the metastore.
Read the first two lines. The files were there the whole time. What changed between them?
Read the 2026-11-08 lines, then the last line. How did Spark know which files to open?

code.title: MetastoreDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.bigdata.l03.demo import org.apache.spark.sql.SaveMode import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.col import java.io.File /** * Registers the lake from PartitionPruningDemo as a table in Spark's catalog, which plays the Hive * metastore here, and shows that the catalog's partition list and the directories can disagree. */ fun main() { val lake = File("build/l03/lake") val spark = demoSpark() File(lake, "dt=2026-11-08").deleteRecursively() // left over from an earlier run if (!File(lake, "_SUCCESS").exists()) { demoPayments(spark).write().mode(SaveMode.Overwrite).partitionBy("dt").parquet(lake.absolutePath) } fun show(label: String, sql: String) = println("%-34s %s".format(label, spark.sql(sql).collectAsList().joinToString(" ") { it.mkString(",") })) // 1. register the existing directory as an external table: schema and location go into the catalog spark.sql(""" CREATE TABLE payments (payment_id BIGINT, merchant_id INT, card_country STRING, amount_cents BIGINT, created_at TIMESTAMP, dt STRING) USING parquet PARTITIONED BY (dt) LOCATION '${lake.absolutePath}'""") show("rows right after CREATE TABLE:", "SELECT count(*) FROM payments") // 2. the catalog has no partitions yet; MSCK REPAIR walks the directory and adds them spark.sql("MSCK REPAIR TABLE payments") show("rows after MSCK REPAIR TABLE:", "SELECT count(*) FROM payments") println("%-34s %d".format("partitions the catalog knows:", spark.sql("SHOW PARTITIONS payments").count())) // 3. a late job writes 2026-11-08 straight into the directory, without telling the catalog demoPayments(spark, days = 1, firstEpochSecond = 1_794_096_000L).drop("dt") .write().mode(SaveMode.Overwrite).parquet(File(lake, "dt=2026-11-08").absolutePath) show("rows for 2026-11-08, before:", "SELECT count(*) FROM payments WHERE dt = '2026-11-08'") spark.sql("ALTER TABLE payments ADD PARTITION (dt = '2026-11-08')") show("rows for 2026-11-08, after ADD:", "SELECT count(*) FROM payments WHERE dt = '2026-11-08'") // 4. a filter on dt is answered by the catalog first: only one day's files get opened val oneDay = spark.table("payments").where(col("dt").equalTo("2026-11-03")) println("files opened for dt = 2026-11-03: %d of %d".format(oneDay.inputFiles().size, dataFiles(lake).size)) spark.stop() }

try.expect:
rows right after CREATE TABLE:     0
rows after MSCK REPAIR TABLE:      70000
partitions the catalog knows:      7
rows for 2026-11-08, before:       0
rows for 2026-11-08, after ADD:    10000
files opened for dt = 2026-11-03:   1 of 10

The new table saw no rows until the repair registered its seven partitions. The late day stayed invisible until ADD PARTITION. The last line comes from inputFiles(), the list of files Spark's scan will open after it asked the catalog which partitions match: 1 of the 10 files now in the lake.

sections.html:
Hive tables are built from files and directories, and the cracks are in exactly those places.

A write is not atomic, meaning readers can see it half done. A job that writes a day as 200 files doesn't publish them in one step. Depending on how the job commits its output, they appear task by task or file by file, and a query that lists the directory in between sees part of the day. INSERT OVERWRITE, Hive's statement for replacing a partition's contents, is worse: it removes the old files and then moves the new ones in, so a reader at the wrong moment sees nothing. Two jobs writing the same partition can mix their files. The metastore can't help, because it tracks directories, not files.

Listing stays slow, even with the metastore. The metastore knows which directories to read, but not the files inside them, so the engine still lists each directory it reads. With 1,000 names per request, a partition that holds 50,000 files takes 50 requests, one after another, before the first byte of data arrives.

Small files cost more than their bytes. Every file means an open, a read of its footer (the index Parquet keeps at the end of each file), and on S3 a request with its own latency. A streaming job that writes a file into its partition every minute turns one day into 1,440 files. The demo below shows the effect on your own SSD, where opening a file is cheap. On S3 the gap is wider.

These are the problems that Iceberg and Delta Lake were built to solve. Both are table formats: a set of metadata files, stored next to the data, that list every data file of the table (lessons 9 and 10). Because the table lists its files, nobody lists directories. A write becomes visible in one atomic step, when a new snapshot replaces the old one. (A snapshot is a complete list of the table's files at one moment.) Readers see all of a write or none of it. And you can partition by days(created_at) without a separate dt column. The metastore lives on in that world too: Iceberg can use it as its catalog, and Hive's own docs describe an Iceberg REST catalog backed by the metastore. New builds lean toward REST catalogs, catalogs that speak a standard HTTP API, which lesson 10 covers.

try.title: Store the same week as 7 files and as 350
steps: Run SmallFilesDemo. It writes the same 70,000 payments twice: one file per day, then 50 files per day.
Predict: the data is identical. How much slower is the second layout to query?
Compare the sizes too. Why is the many-files copy bigger?

code.title: SmallFilesDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.bigdata.l03.demo import java.io.File import java.sql.Connection import java.sql.DriverManager /** The same week of payments stored as 7 files and as 350 small ones, then queried the same way. */ fun main() { DriverManager.getConnection("jdbc:duckdb:").use { c -> // 70,000 payments, 10,000 a day for 7 days c.run("""CREATE TABLE payments AS SELECT i AS payment_id, (hash(i) % 250000 + 100)::BIGINT AS amount_cents, DATE '2026-11-01' + (i // 10000)::INTEGER AS dt FROM range(70000) t(i)""") val few = fresh("build/l03/few-files") val many = fresh("build/l03/many-files") for (day in 0 until 7) { val dt = "2026-11-0${day + 1}" // one file per day, as a daily batch job would write it c.copy("SELECT payment_id, amount_cents FROM payments WHERE dt = DATE '$dt'", File(few, "dt=$dt/part-0.parquet")) // 50 files per day, as a job with 50 tasks (or a stream writing every half hour) would for (part in 0 until 50) { c.copy("SELECT payment_id, amount_cents FROM payments WHERE dt = DATE '$dt' AND payment_id % 50 = $part", File(many, "dt=$dt/part-$part.parquet")) } } for (root in listOf(few, many)) { val sql = "SELECT dt, sum(amount_cents) FROM read_parquet('${root.absolutePath}/**/*.parquet') GROUP BY dt" val best = (1..5).minOf { val t0 = System.nanoTime() c.createStatement().use { s -> s.executeQuery(sql).use { rs -> while (rs.next()) Unit } } (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1e6 } val files = root.walkTopDown().filter { it.name.endsWith(".parquet") }.toList() println("%-10s %4d files, %4.1f MB, query %5.1f ms".format(root.name, files.size, files.sumOf { it.length() } / 1e6, best)) } } } private fun fresh(path: String) = File(path).apply { deleteRecursively(); mkdirs() } private fun Connection.run(sql: String) = createStatement().use { it.execute(sql) } private fun Connection.copy(select: String, file: File) { file.parentFile.mkdirs() run("COPY ($select) TO '${file.absolutePath}' (FORMAT parquet)") }

try.expect:
few-files     7 files,  0.6 MB, query   1.6 ms
many-files  350 files,  0.8 MB, query  18.3 ms

The times vary a little between runs (19.9 ms on a second run here), but the many-files layout is always about ten times slower for the same rows. It is also bigger, because every Parquet file repeats its own footer and schema, and smaller files compress worse. Here each extra file costs a local open; on S3 each one is another request.

analogy: A Hive table works like a library with a card catalog. The catalog (the metastore) says which shelf holds which year's books (the partitions). A librarian looks up the card before walking to a shelf, so a question about 2024 never visits the 2019 shelf. If someone shelves a new year of books without writing a card, nobody finds them until a librarian walks every shelf and writes the missing cards (MSCK REPAIR TABLE). The analogy breaks at the cards: a library catalog lists every book, while the metastore only lists shelves. It can't tell you that a shelf is half full because someone is still putting books on it.
world: Settlement exports often end up in exactly this shape. A nightly job writes settlements/dt=2026-11-07/ to S3, and finance reads it with Athena (AWS's hosted SQL engine) or Trino, through Glue (AWS's catalog service, which Hive-compatible engines can use in place of a metastore) or a Hive metastore. Two things from this lesson bite there. The job that writes the directory has to register the partition, or the dashboard shows an empty day until someone notices. And a re-run of the job for a day replaces files while a dashboard may be reading them. The Hive-era fix is to write the re-run to a new directory, then point the partition at it in one metastore call: ALTER TABLE settlements PARTITION (dt = '2026-11-07') SET LOCATION '...'. Readers then see either the old day or the new one, never half of each.
mistake: The common mistake is filtering on the timestamp instead of the partition column. WHERE created_at >= '2026-11-01' reads like the right filter and returns the right rows, so nobody notices that the engine opened every file in the table. The plan tells you. In Spark, PartitionFilters: [] on the FileScan line means no pruning. In DuckDB, a missing Scanning Files: n/m line means the same. Put the partition column in the WHERE clause too (dt >= '2026-11-01' AND created_at >= ...), or move to a table format with hidden partitioning.

compare.title: The same daily-partitioned table in Oracle and in Hive

a.label: Oracle: schema on write
a.title: Oracle: schema on write
a.html: CREATE TABLE payments ( payment_id NUMBER(19) PRIMARY KEY, amount_cents NUMBER(19) NOT NULL, created_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL ) PARTITION BY RANGE (created_at) INTERVAL (NUMTODSINTERVAL(1, 'DAY')) (PARTITION p0 VALUES LESS THAN (TIMESTAMP '2026-11-01 00:00:00')); INSERT INTO payments VALUES (3000, '12.50 EUR', SYSTIMESTAMP); -- rejected at INSERT time with ORA-01722: the bad row never lands

b.label: Hive: schema on read
b.title: Hive: schema on read
b.html: CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE payments ( payment_id BIGINT, amount_cents BIGINT, created_at TIMESTAMP ) PARTITIONED BY (dt STRING) STORED AS PARQUET LOCATION 's3a://lake/payments/'; -- a job copies batch-4.parquet into s3a://lake/payments/dt=2026-11-08/; nothing checks it ALTER TABLE payments ADD PARTITION (dt = '2026-11-08'); SELECT sum(amount_cents) FROM payments WHERE dt = '2026-11-08'; -- only now does a reader hit the file whose amount_cents is a string

compare.note: Both tables are partitioned by day and both prune. The difference is who owns the files. Oracle writes its own data files, checks every row on the way in, and knows which rows each partition holds, so the partition key can be created_at itself and a filter on created_at prunes. Hive owns only the description. Files arrive from anywhere, the partition key is a separate dt column that lives in the path, and a bad file is found by the first query that reads it.

worked.title: Lay out an authorizations table for a fraud team

steps.say: The fraud team asks two kinds of questions: daily totals for the last week, and everything one merchant did in the last 30 days. You keep 3 years at about 4 million authorizations a day. Start by counting directories and file sizes for each candidate layout.
steps.code:
// 1. 4,000,000 rows a day x ~40 bytes compressed = ~160 MB a day; 3 years = 1,095 days
dt only:             1,095 directories, ~160 MB each
dt + card_country:   1,095 x 30 = 32,850 directories, ~5 MB each
dt + merchant_id:    1,095 x 50,000 = 54,750,000 directories, ~3 KB each

steps.say: Pick dt alone. The merchant question is real, but partitioning by merchant explodes the file count. Instead, sort each day's rows by merchant, so the min/max statistics inside each file let a reader skip most of it (lesson 4 shows how).
steps.code: // 2. one directory per day, rows sorted by merchant inside each file authorizations .repartition(col("dt")) // all rows of a day in one task: one file per day .sortWithinPartitions("dt", "merchant_id", "created_at") // dt first, as the writer needs .write().mode(SaveMode.Overwrite) .partitionBy("dt") .parquet("s3a://lake/authorizations/")

steps.say: Register the table once. After that, the writing job adds its own partition right after each daily write, so you never depend on a slow repair over S3.
steps.code: -- 3. once CREATE TABLE authorizations ( auth_id BIGINT, merchant_id INT, card_id BIGINT, amount_cents BIGINT, created_at TIMESTAMP, dt STRING) USING parquet PARTITIONED BY (dt) LOCATION 's3a://lake/authorizations/'; -- after each daily write, from the same job ALTER TABLE authorizations ADD IF NOT EXISTS PARTITION (dt = '2026-11-07');

steps.say: Query with the partition column in the filter, and keep the merchant filter for the reader to use inside the files. Check the plan once: PartitionFilters should list the dt range.
steps.code: -- 4. dt prunes directories; merchant_id prunes inside files SELECT count(*), sum(amount_cents) FROM authorizations WHERE dt BETWEEN '2026-10-09' AND '2026-11-07' AND merchant_id = 4711;

lab.title: A Hive-style payments lake, read two ways
steps: Run the tests. All five fail at writeByDay, because every test needs the lake first.
Write writeByDay with partitionBy("dt"). The first test checks the directory names, then reads one file on its own to prove dt isn't inside it.
Write registerTable: a CREATE TABLE with the column list from the KDoc, USING parquet PARTITIONED BY (dt) LOCATION '...', then a call to refreshPartitions.
Write refreshPartitions. Its test writes a late day straight to disk, checks that the table can't see it, calls your function, and checks again.
Write dailyTotal. The test calls inputFiles() on your query and expects only that day's files.
Write dailyTotalSql for DuckDB. The test runs EXPLAIN on your SQL and reads the Scanning Files: n/m line. Run all five tests until they pass.
hints: A table created over existing directories starts with no partitions. MSCK REPAIR TABLE name adds them; Spark also accepts REPAIR TABLE name.
spark.table(table).where(col("dt").equalTo(dt)).agg(sum("amount_cents")). A filter on to_date(col("created_at")) gives the right total and fails the file test.
In DuckDB, read_parquet('<root>/**/*.parquet', hive_partitioning = true) turns dt=... into a column. DuckDB reads it as a DATE, and WHERE dt = '2026-11-05' still works.

drill.title: Register a lake, then skip the catalog
drill.prompt: From memory, write the Spark SQL that turns an existing dt= directory tree of Parquet payments into a queryable table, and the statement that registers one new day later. Then write the DuckDB query that answers "total for one day" from the same files with no catalog at all.

answer.html: -- Spark: the catalog owns the schema and the partition list CREATE TABLE payments (payment_id BIGINT, amount_cents BIGINT, created_at TIMESTAMP, dt STRING) USING parquet PARTITIONED BY (dt) LOCATION '/data/lake/payments'; MSCK REPAIR TABLE payments; -- learn the days already on disk ALTER TABLE payments ADD PARTITION (dt = '2026-11-08'); -- later: one new day -- DuckDB: no catalog, the paths are the partition list SELECT sum(amount_cents) FROM read_parquet('/data/lake/payments/**/*.parquet', hive_partitioning = true) WHERE dt = '2026-11-08';

recap: A Hive table is a directory of files plus a description (schema, format, location) kept in the metastore. Files are checked only when a query reads them: schema on read.
Partitions are subdirectories named key=value. The value lives in the path, and a filter on the partition column lets an engine skip whole directories.
Pruning works only on the partition column. A filter on created_at opens every file of a dt-partitioned table.
The metastore's partition list is the truth. A directory written behind its back stays invisible until ALTER TABLE ... ADD PARTITION or MSCK REPAIR TABLE.
The model breaks at the file level: writes aren't atomic, listing is slow on object storage, and small files cost more than their bytes. Iceberg and Delta fix exactly these.

explain.prompt: A data engineer asks why a move to Iceberg is worth it, since "Hive partitions already prune". Explain what Hive-style partitioning does well and two problems it can't fix.
explain.answer: Hive-style partitioning does one thing well. If a query filters on the partition column, the engine asks the metastore for the matching partitions and lists only those directories. A one-day query on a three-year table reads a thousandth of it. Two problems are out of its reach because the metastore tracks directories, not files. First, writes aren't atomic: a job adds files one by one, so a reader can see half a write, and an overwrite can show an empty partition. Second, the engine has to list directories to find files, which is slow on S3 with 1,000 keys per request, and it gets worse as small files pile up. There's also a usability trap: pruning only works on the separate dt column, so a filter on created_at silently reads everything. Iceberg keeps its own list of every file, commits a snapshot atomically, and partitions by a transform of created_at itself.

deeper.html:
Hive had a second layout trick besides partitions: buckets. Inside each partition, rows can be spread across a fixed number of files by a hash of a column, so bucket 7 of card_id always holds the same cards. The Hive paper describes it: each bucket is one file in the partition directory.

Bucketing is a shuffle paid for at write time. Lesson 2's partitioner sends each key to reducer hash(key) mod R; bucketing does the same with R buckets and keeps the result on disk. Say two tables are bucketed on the same key into the same number of buckets. A join can then match bucket 7 of one with bucket 7 of the other, and no rows have to move across the network.

Spark offers this for its own tables with bucketBy(n, column) together with saveAsTable. The modern version lives in table formats. Spark's tuning guide describes a storage-partitioned join that uses the partition layout of a table format such as Iceberg. When it applies there is no Exchange (Spark's name for a shuffle) before the join at all. The catch is the same in every era: both sides must agree on the key and the bucket count, and a bucket layout that matches today's join rarely matches next year's.
